title: All Souls (2 November)
hookLine: many churches remember all the faithful departed, and families visit graves

lines: A CANDLE IN A RED GLASS JAR.
cards: Dusk in a cemetery. A woman kneels and pulls weeds from around a stone, then wipes the name with her sleeve. Her son sets a candle in a red glass jar at the foot of the grave and shields the match from the wind.
Across the rows, little flames come on, one by one, until the whole hillside flickers. Someone has brought a thermos. Nobody is in a hurry.
In some countries, this is the second of November. Yesterday the church remembered the saints. Today it remembers everyone else who has died in faith.

teach.b: All Saints and All Souls sit side by side on purpose. One day for the cloud of witnesses; the next for the faithful departed: grandparents, friends, a child, the people whose graves we know. Grief comes first.
At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, the King James Bible says it in two words: "Jesus wept." He knows what he's about to do, and he weeps anyway. In the story, grief isn't a lack of faith.
Earlier in that chapter, the hope: "I am the resurrection, and the life." Paul holds both when he writes to Thessalonica about the dead. He doesn't tell them not to grieve.
He tells them "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." Sorrow, with hope in it. Churches keep this day differently.
Catholics pray for the dead, trusting that God's mercy can still be at work in them, purifying them, and on this day Masses are offered for all the faithful departed.
Orthodox Christians pray for the departed too, in memorial services through the year.
Protestant churches differ: some don't pray for the dead, and instead give thanks for their lives and entrust them to God; some, including some Anglicans, keep All Souls with prayers.
In some places, families clean the graves and light candles. The carry comes from an old Western prayer asking God to give the dead eternal rest and perpetual light.
In Latin it begins with the word requiem, rest, which is why a Mass for the dead is called a requiem. Rest, and light, asked for those we can't hold anymore.

how: On All Souls, Catholics and some Anglicans pray for the faithful departed and offer Masses or services for them; in some countries families clean and decorate graves and light candles, and some churches read out the names of those who died in the past year.

o: a day for baptizing new members of the church
a day for giving thanks for the year's newborns
a day to remember all the faithful who have died

games.q: two days, side by side — tap the pairs.

s: in the Bible, grief is a sign of weak faith
Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, and Paul says sorrow, but not as those with no hope.
all churches pray for the dead in the same way
Catholics and Orthodox pray for the departed; some Protestants give thanks for them instead.
a requiem is named for the old prayer's first word
requiem, rest: eternal rest grant unto them.

games.q: you're Jesus, at the tomb of your friend Lazarus. you know you're about to call him out. what does John say you do first?
o: go straight in without a word.
games.why: Jesus wept. grief and hope in the same chapter: then, I am the resurrection, and the life.

practice: Light a candle if you can, safely, or switch on a small lamp, and bring to mind one person who has died: say their name, and let one ordinary memory come, their laugh, a phrase they always used. Let whatever you feel be there.
If you pray, use the old words, rest eternal grant unto them, and let light shine on them; if not, watch the flame and hold them in it.

wordCard.voice: All Souls. The day after All Saints, when churches remember all the faithful departed, and families visit graves and light candles.

orig.note: Latin: rest. the first word of the Western church's old prayer for the dead, and the name of a Mass for the dead.

carryVoice: Your line: rest eternal. Grief and hope, sitting side by side in the candlelight. Until tomorrow.
